newsitem.title: UK: Cross winds buffet dollar in Europe but data buoys.
newsitem.headline: Cross winds buffet dollar in Europe but data buoys.

text.p: The dollar stumbled in late Europe as the mark sharpened its assault on the lira, after a session which saw the U.S. unit largely at the mercy of cross moves.

The dollar was unsettled in early trade as mark/yen slid to fresh eight-month lows, though the cross later recovered ground. Rumours -- later denied -- of an imminent announcement that European monetary union was to be delayed also boosted the mark.
But a batch of U.S. data, most of which matched or exceeded expectations, buoyed the dollar as they kept market speculation of a U.S. interest rate increase on the boil, analysts said.

"Apart from the GDP, the rest of the data clearly showed the U.S. economy has got quite a momentum going in the early part of 1997, and that's going to keep the market on edge about a possible rate hike," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International. "That's giving good support to the dollar."
U.S. fourth-quarter GDP growth was revised down to 3.9 percent from the previous estimate of 4.7, undershooting consensus expectations of 4.1.
But the February University of Michigan sentiment index topped forecasts, rising to 99.7 from 97.4, while the Chicago purchasing managers' index rose to 56.2 from January's 55.9.
U.S. January existing home sales were broadly in line with expectations, increasing 2.1 percent to 3.94 million.

Analysts said the focus was now on next week's February U.S. non-farm payrolls data, with a strong number to stoke talk of Fed tightening. The second part of Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony will also transfix the markets.
The first leg of the testimony spooked markets with its talk of inflation risks and buoyant equity markets.
"I don't think he'll change the overall tone...his speech will be pretty hawkish, saying the Fed's about to push the trigger, but not just yet," said Stamenkovic.
The lira swooped to three-month lows around 1002.25 per mark in late Europe, riding roughshod over perceived Bank of Italy attempts to halt the rout by selling marks for lire.
Mark/lira ended around 994.00/35 in Europe on Thursday.

The peseta also felt the heat, falling to 84.95/97 per mark by 1705 GMT from late yesterday's 84.77/80. Dealers said the Bank of Spain had intervened in the European morning, buying pesetas for marks at around 84.85/90.
Sliding Club Med debt did the lira and peseta no favours.
"Italian and Spanish bond markets have taken a huge whack today," said Robert Prior, economist at HSBC James Capel.

Mark/yen was a major mover in early Europe, sinking to an eight-month trough of 71.14 as the Japanese currency firmed across the board. It recovered, though, to 71.60/63 by 1708 GMT, above late yesterday's European level of 71.45/48.

Analysts said comments by Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita giving a more upbeat assessment of Japan's economy had combined with ongoing concerns about fund repatriation by Japanese investors ahead of fiscal year-end to boost the yen.
"These sort of fears are helping to keep the dollar a bit on the defensive against the yen," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets in London.

On a broader outlook, there remains no reason to short dollars dramatically, said Stretch. "The fundamental picture hasn't changed vis-a-vis the U.S. being positive and Japanese economic fundamentals still fairly soft," he said.

Sterling had a choppy session. It tripped in early Europe after the Wirral by-election brought victory to the opposition Labour party and sent the Conservative government into a minority, before recouping its losses. But dollar/mark's late weakness sobered the pound, which ended at 2.7480/90 marks and $1.6292/02 compared to late Thursday's levels here of 2.7470/75 and $1.6290/00.
-- Abigail Levene, London forex +44-171-542-8968
